resumen: Why a photo comes out orange or bluish and how to make whites come out white.

bloques.alt: Three drawings of the same white cup. On the left, under bulb light left uncorrected, the whole scene leans orange: 1, orange. In the middle, with white balance set right, the cup is white: 2, neutral. On the right, under shade light left uncorrected, the whole scene leans blue: 3, bluish.
bloques.pie: 1 Bulb light, uncorrected: orange. 2 White balance set right: whites come out white. 3 Shade, uncorrected: bluish.

bloques.texto: Light has color, and white balance tells the camera what color it is so whites come out white.
The light of a bulb is orange and the light of the shade is bluish. If the camera doesn't correct it, everything white comes out with that tint. [[balance-de-blancos|White balance]] corrects it.

items: Presets: daylight, cloudy, shade, bulb, fluorescent and flash. Pick the one for the light you have.
Manual: on many cameras you can set the color temperature, in Kelvin.
When auto gets confused: with mixed lights (a window and a bulb).
When you want a color on purpose: a warmer sunset or a cool, bluish feel.
If you set it by hand, remember to go back to auto or to adjust it when the light changes, for example from sun to clouds.

bloques.texto: If you shoot in [[raw|RAW]], you can change the white balance when you edit without losing quality. In [[jpeg|JPEG]] only a small correction fits.
On many phones you change it in the camera's Pro or manual mode, and in some simpler camera apps too.

At home, with a bulb on, take a photo of a white sheet of paper in auto and another with the bulb preset. If your phone doesn't let you change it, compare the paper under the bulb and next to a window.
